newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech markets calm as govt confidence vote looms.
newsitem.headline: Czech markets calm as govt confidence vote looms.

text.p: Czech markets were calm on Tuesday ahead of an expected confidence vote in the government of Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, with analysts saying the market had already built in expectations of a win for the premier's ruling coalition.

The Czech crown strengthened nearly one full percentage point against both the dollar and mark in early trading, while a surge in blue chip shares pushed the Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index up 0.56 percent to 504.2 points.

"Ahead of the confidence vote you see the crown is strengthening as everyone expects the government will win... The market has now discounted a government victory," said Petr Kukla, a currency trader at Girocredit Bank in Prague.
The crown was trading at 32.288 to the dollar and 18.844 against the mark at midday on Tuesday.

Parliament is expected to place the vote at the top of its agenda when it begins meeting on Tuesday at 2.00 p.m. (1200 GMT), though political wrangling by opposition parties may keep the lower house from holding the vote for days.
Klaus's three-party, centre-right coalition controls only 100 seats in the 200-seat parliament and even members of the government have been driving hard bargains for their support in the vote.

Optimism about prospects for a government victory rose on Tuesday morning after the leader of a key coalition party, the Christian Democrats (KDU-CSL), was quoted by CTK news agency as saying he was happy with the outcome of emergency budget talks.
The seven-hour talks focused on how to cut some 20 billion crowns from this year's budget and lasted into Tuesday morning.
With the governing coalition appearing unified before the vote, analysts said investors were cheered that the fate of Klaus and his government's economic programme should be secure.

"We're seeing a bit of a technical correction that started in the market yesterday, but also there's some optimism that the confidence is going to go Klaus's way," said Matt Starr, director of capital markets for Creditanstalt in Prague.
"But whatever upside potential we're seeing here...the market will probably trade down toward the end of the week," he added.
Klaus called the confidence vote last week after several weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets.
Speculators, alarmed at widening current account and trade deficits and growing political uncertainty, sold the crown short, causing the central bank to float the currency on May 27.
Coalition leaders agreed the next day to a sweeping cabinet reshuffle and the austerity programme, which called for budget cuts and wage freezes.
Jiri Krovak, chief economist for fixed income brokerage WoodCommerz, said he thinks the chances of Klaus's government winning the vote are about 50-50 given the slim majority .
"It's not clear to me as of yet whether all individuals in the (coalition) will vote in favour of the government," he said.
"If the government did lose the vote, there would certainly be an immediate negative effect on the market, the market would take this as a very bad piece of news," Krovak added.
If Klaus loses the vote, analysts say he would be obliged under the constitution to step down.
If President Vaclav Havel was then unable to broker a workable government, early elections would be called. A general vote is not scheduled until the spring of 2000.
Klaus called the vote partly to head off a non-confidence vote called by the opposition Social Democrats (CSSD), led by Klaus's arch enemy Milos Zeman.
